ethiopia.title: Ethiopia fighting escalates in Tigray killing 52 civilians, medic tells the BBC
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia fighting escalates in Tigray killing 52 civilians in Alamata, medic tells the BBC - BBC News BBC Homepage Skip to content Accessibility Help Your account Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds More menu More menu Search BBC Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds Close menu BBC News Menu Home Climate World US & Canada UK Business Tech Science Entertainment & Arts Health More In Pictures BBC Verify Newsbeat World Africa Asia Australia Europe Latin America Middle East Ethiopia fighting escalates in Tigray killing 52 civilians, medic tells the BBC Image source, Social media via Reuters Image caption, Tanks and armoured vehicles were filmed passing through Alamata after days of clashes By Michael Teferi , BBC Africa , Lion Tsigab , BBC Tigrinya and Lucy Fleming Published 30 September 2026 At least 52 civilians have been killed during three days of heavy fighting around Alamata in Ethiopia's northern Tigray region, hospital sources have told the BBC. It appears government troops have taken control of the town from regional fighters and intend to push north towards Mekelle, the region's main city. Social media clips show army tanks on Alamata's streets. Clashes broke out last week after months of tension between the government and the party that controls Tigray, with both accusing each other of violating a 2022 deal that ended a two-year civil war. Fighting has also affected neighbouring regions with 33 tourists stranded for the last week in Lalibela, a Unesco world heritage site. "We have heard fighting, gunfire and artillery cannons firing throughout the week," a British tourist, who asked not to be named, told the BBC's Newsday programme about clashes near Lalibela in the Amhara region. He said there was a large military presence in Lalibela, famous for being home to 13th Century churches hewn from rock and a holy site for millions of Orthodox Christians. Most visitors to the tourist hub had been unable to leave since the airport closed to commercial flights last Wednesday, though he said 14 Israeli tourists had been evacuated by military helicopter on Monday. The fighting around Lalibela has involved the army and an Amhara militia that has allied with Tigrayan fighters. Earlier in September, they joined forces with other Ethiopian armed movements to form a seven-member alliance with the stated intention of removing the government in the capital, Addis Ababa. There is also a fear that neighbouring Eritrea could be drawn into the conflict - as the government accuses Asmara of supporting the armed groups, something it denies. The BBC is unable to report from Tigray and surrounding areas and it is difficult to find out what is happening because communications to the region have been cut. The two sides disagree over who started the latest fighting. Are Ethiopians marching back to war in Tigray? Published 5 days ago WATCH: Why are Ethiopia's rebels joining forces? Published 2 days ago The Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), the party that runs Tigray, says it was responding to a federal offensive, including drone strikes, while the government says Tigrayan forces attacked first after seizing control of airports in the region. TPLF fighters are also fighting in the Afar region, in a strategic area which connects landlocked Ethiopia to Djibouti and its ports. Over the last few days, medical charity Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) said more than 700 wounded people had been admitted to hospitals it supports in Tigray. The doctor at Alamata General Hospital, who requested anonymity, told the BBC the fighting in and around the town had taken place between Saturday and Monday, and involved heavy explosives and artillery, some of which landed in residential homes. Those killed in the crossfire included children as young as three days old, mothers and cattle herders. Twelve people had died in a single strike on the town's marketplace, the medic said. Since the fighting erupted, banking services in Tigray have been suspended by the government. Access to the internet has also been cut - though it is not clear who ordered the closure. A separate source in Alamata told the BBC there was a worsening humanitarian crisis in the area, as the town swelled with people fleeing fighting. "All the residents of the surrounding areas entered the town of Alamata by walking on foot for as long as an hour, hoping the town would be safe. "Unfortunately, everything is blocked - no banking service, no money transfer, no power, no internet, no phone. Hence people are in crisis, simply suffering, everyone is desperate and frustrated." The British tourist in Lalibela said online banking was working in Lalibela but there was a shortage of physical cash. He said the situation around the town had calmed down in the last two days and there were indications the airport, which was still being used by the military, might reopen on Thursday. "The local people, they are still scared of what might happen. The military presence here in the town has remained and a larger military force has been seen leaving the town heading north," he said. When the airport was first closed, 53 tourists had been in the town, he explained. But some had since been evacuated, including the 14 Israelis airlifted out on Monday while another five had left the day before via an NGO convoy, despite advice not to travel by road. Of the remaining tourists in Lalibela, the largest group were Americans, with Israelis, Britons, South Korean, South Africans, an Ethiopian-New Zealander and a Mexican also stranded, he said. Meanwhile, for those cut off in Tigray because of the telecoms shutdown, the Tigray Broadcasting Service (TBS), based in Addis Ababa, has started an initiative to help reconnect families. The broadcaster has said it will collect video messages via its Telegram channel from people outside the region and air them via satellite TV. While limited to greetings and updates, this will provide a rare lifeline for families separated by the blackout. The clampdown on Tigray's banking services is also affecting Tigrayans who are not physically in the region. Customers have told the BBC that bank accounts opened in Tigray have been frozen or restricted. "I boarded public transport from Addis Ababa to Adama and tried to pay using a mobile transfer, but it didn't work," said a former Mekelle resident who moved to the capital two months ago because of growing tensions in Tigray. "It has created havoc for many people like me who escaped the situation in Tigray," he told the BBC's Tigrinya service. "Many Tigrayans are now in trouble." Why are Ethiopia's rebels joining forces? Close Seven rebel groups from across Ethiopia have announced a new alliance against Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's government. Some were once rivals, others fought separately, but they now say they're united by a common goal. So, who are they, and why have they joined forces now, just as fighting has flared once more in the northern Tigray region? ethiopia.title: Are Ethiopians marching back to war in Tigray?
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia fighting: Are Tigray's TPLF forces and the army heading back to war? - BBC News BBC Homepage Skip to content Accessibility Help Your account Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds More menu More menu Search BBC Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds Close menu BBC News Menu Home Climate World US & Canada UK Business Tech Science Entertainment & Arts Health More In Pictures BBC Verify Newsbeat World Africa Asia Australia Europe Latin America Middle East Are Ethiopians marching back to war in Tigray? Image source, Reuters Image caption, Tigrayan forces have been patrolling the streets of Tigray's capital, Mekelle, this week By Lucy Fleming and BBC Africa Published 26 September 2026 Fighting has erupted in Ethiopia's northern region of Tigray between regional forces and the national army. Tigray residents, who have been trying to recover from a brutal two-year war that ended in 2022, fear a return to full-scale conflict. There are reports of panic buying - and now internet and call services have been disrupted. This means people cannot get access to their money via digital apps in what has become a largely cashless society after ATMs stopped working several months ago. Why has fighting broken out now? It follows more than six months of worsening relations between the government and the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), the party that runs Tigray. The African Union (AU) brokered a peace deal, known as the Pretoria Agreement, between the two sides, ending the war nearly four years ago - but several issues have remained unresolved that have inflamed tensions. This year, both sides have been trading blame while troops have mobilised amid pockets of fighting. This week, major clashes erupted in Tigray and quickly spread into the neighbouring Afar and Amhara regions. The two sides disagree over who started the latest escalation. The TPLF says it was responding to a federal offensive, including drone strikes, while the government says Tigrayan forces attacked first after seizing control of airports in Tigray. Who are the TPLF? For much of Tigray's modern political history, it has been governed by the TPLF, which first emerged as an armed movement in the 1970s fighting Ethiopia's military government. It became a major force in the overthrow of the Marxist regime in 1991 and went on to become the most powerful component of the Ethiopian People's Revolutionary Democratic Front (EPRDF), the coalition that governed the ethnically diverse country for nearly three decades. At times this proved contentious as some felt the TPLF held too much sway as Tigrayans only make up around 6% of Ethiopia's population. When Abiy Ahmed became prime minister in 2018, he replaced the EPRDF with the Prosperity Party, significantly watering down the TPLF's influence. Relations between Addis Ababa and the TPLF rapidly deteriorated until war erupted in 2020 in what was one of the most deadly conflicts this century. The AU mediator estimated some 600,000 people died during the war, which totally cut off Tigray from the outside world and drove the region to the precipice of famine. An uneasy truce was agreed in November 2022. Why has the peace deal faltered? There are four key issues - and two concern the fertile area of western Tigray. The TPLF lost control of this territory in the early days of the war to Amhara, a region which neighbours Tigray to the west and whose fighters had fought on the side of the Ethiopian army. Many people in Amhara believe the territory of western Tigray should never have been incorporated into Tigray when regional boundaries were redrawn after the military regime was ousted in 1991. When its fighters seized control during the recent civil war, hundreds of thousands of ethnic Tigrayan people fled and are now living in homeless camps in Tigray and in the capital, Addis Ababa. The TPLF wants western Tigray back and for those displaced from the territory to return. The government says the future of the territory needs to be decided by a referendum. Image source, Reuters Image caption, People have been reportedly rushing to buy food, panicking that a full-blown war will start For the government, a major matter of contention has been disarmament. It says the TPLF has only handed over old weaponry to the AU and has been hiding its arms. The two sides have also been at loggerheads over how Tigray should be governed. Under the terms of the deal, an interim administration was appointed by Abiy. But attempts by the prime minister to influence affairs caused disputes within the TPLF itself and just before the general election in May, which was not held in Tigray because of the security situation, it restored its pre-war administration, disbanding the one set up by Abiy. This has meant that civil servants are longer being paid and other services have been seizing up, worsening economic conditions. Who is backing the TPLF? A major development has seen the TPLF, once politically isolated inside Ethiopia, gain several key allies. Earlier in September, it joined six other armed movements in forming what is called the Alliance for Survival, which includes those actively fighting the government like Amhara's Fano militia and the Oromo Liberation Army. Members of the new alliance have different grievances, but they do share one objective: they want to remove Abiy's government from power. So while the TPLF and Fano forces were on opposite sides during the civil war - and still disagree over the fate of western Tigray - they have temporarily put some of their differences aside. TPLF officials say they do not want to repeat the situation of 2020, when they felt surrounded and isolated. Yet analysts caution the alliance may become difficult to maintain because its members ultimately have very different interests. What is the government's position? As well as blaming the TPLF for starting the recent fighting, it has criticised the new alliance, portraying it as an attempt to destabilise the country. It has also accused Eritrea of supporting armed groups inside Ethiopia, something Asmara denies. During the recent civil war, Eritrea fought alongside Ethiopian troops but the two neighbours, which have long had a volatile relationship, have again fallen out. Their disagreement centres on the Red Sea and its ports. Ethiopia, the world's most populous landlocked nation, lost access to them when Eritrea seceded in 1993. Recently Prime Minister Abiy has been pushing for ownership of Eritrea's southern port of Assab - about 60km (37 miles) from the border - and hinted at taking it by force. What do we know about the bombing in Tigray? Reports indicate that federal forces have been using drones and other military operations against Tigrayan forces. The government's stated justification is that it is responding to attacks and trying to defend federal positions and territory. However, the circumstances surrounding individual strikes are difficult to independently verify. Residents in one recently targeted town told the BBC the drones had hit two schools, which local officials said had been used by Ethiopian troops as military bases during the war. This suggests Addis Ababa may believe they are again being used for a military purpose - by Tigrayan forces. The attacks have come amid reports that the TPLF has been forcibly recruiting young men to join its ranks. What is being done to stop the fighting? The main diplomatic effort is being led by the AU, which has called for an immediate cessation of hostilities and a return to direct talks. It has asked former Nigerian President Olusegun Obasanjo, the AU's special Horn of Africa envoy, to engage the parties urgently. The UN has made a similar appeal, warning against a wider and more devastating conflict. The regional organisation Igad has also called for fighting to stop and dialogue to resume. The difficulty is that trust between Addis Ababa and Tigray is extremely low, while the formation of the new armed alliance has made the situation more complicated. Could the fighting spread? Figure caption, Tigray capital "out of cash" as fighting escalates Yes, there is a significant risk of wider conflict inside Ethiopia. The fighting has already moved to areas over and along Tigray's borders, while the government is simultaneously dealing with armed conflicts in other regions, particularly Amhara and Oromia. The new alliance potentially connects several of these conflicts politically and militarily. There is also a fear that Eritrea could be drawn in again - this time against the government. The two aggressors in Sudan's civil war are also on opposite sides when it comes to allegiances in Tigray, potentially complicating matters. The AU has specifically urged all neighbouring countries not to take actions that could further escalate the crisis. ethiopia.title: Internet restricted after fighting breaks out in Ethiopia's Tigray region
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia war: Internet disrupted in Tigray - BBC News BBC Homepage Skip to content Accessibility Help Your account Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds More menu More menu Search BBC Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds Close menu BBC News Menu Home Climate World US & Canada UK Business Tech Science Entertainment & Arts Health More In Pictures BBC Verify Newsbeat World Africa Asia Australia Europe Latin America Middle East Internet restricted after fighting breaks out in Ethiopia's Tigray region Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, The internet was cut in Tigray during the two-year civil war which ended in 2022 (file photo) By Kaleb Moges , BBC Africa and Ondiro Oganga Published 25 September 2026 Internet and call services have been disrupted in Ethiopia's northern region of Tigray following the outbreak of fighting this week between regional forces and the national army. Services provided by state-owned telecoms operator Ethio Telecom have been completely cut, although those from the smaller private firm Safaricom remain operational. Internet monitoring group NetBlocks earlier posted on X that network data indicated a sub-national internet shutdown in northern Tigray. "Last night telecommunications got knocked out," Duke Burbridge, an American humanitarian worker in Tigray's capital, Mekelle, told the BBC's Newsday programme. The BBC has contacted Ethiopia's authorities for comment. Sources have told the Reuters news agency that the group which controls Tigray, the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), ordered the communications blackout, with one suggesting it was to disrupt government drones. The TPLF has not commented. The BBC is unable to report from Tigray and surrounding areas. Even before the current disruption, finding video and images to establish what is happening on the ground has been a challenge. So far, other than footage from Mekelle, most of what has been shared online has been from outside the region. The young women who fought in Ethiopia's last civil war and don't want to see another one Published 6 March Burbridge said there had been a scarcity of cash in Tigray for the past eight months, with people unable to access ATMs so the lack of internet services would be "devastating for everybody". Many people rely on banking and mobile money applications for transactions, with the majority using Ethio Telecom and Safaricom's networks to access these services. On Thursday a Mekelle resident who we are only identifying as Fitsum made a similar point. He told the BBC "there is almost no cash" in the city. With the outbreak of war, people were limiting their movements and the city was all quiet - "it's like a curfew has been placed," he said. Figure caption, Tigray capital 'out of cash' as fighting escalates Clashes between Tigrayan forces and their allies and Ethiopia's federal troops broke out on Wednesday, prompting fears of a return to a full scale civil war and reports of panic buying. A humanitarian source in the neighbouring region of Afar told the AFP news agency there was "heavy fighting overnight", including drone strikes, around the town of Abala in the mountains between Afar and Tigray, as "federal forces pushed the rebels from entering the town". There have also been reports of fighting near the town of Lalibela in the Amhara region, which is home to churches hewn out of rock, recognised as a UN World Heritage site. The US has warned against travel to all three regions. During the two-year conflict which ended in 2022, Tigray was totally cut off from the outside world. Limited access to cash, food and medicine pushed hundreds of thousands into famine-like conditions. It was one of the most deadly conflicts this century - with estimates that some 600,000 people died as the fighting drove the region to the precipice of famine. On Sunday, the TPLF announced an alliance with six other armed groups to oust the government. On Wednesday, its forces seized control of three airports from federal police. Following the seizure of the airports, Ethiopian Airlines has cancelled all flights to Tigray. ethiopia.content: Aliko Dangote, Ethiopia and Djibouti to build $600m fuel pipeline - BBC News BBC Homepage Skip to content Accessibility Help Your account Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds More menu More menu Search BBC Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds Close menu BBC News Menu Home Climate World US & Canada UK Business Tech Science Entertainment & Arts Health More In Pictures BBC Verify Newsbeat World Africa Asia Australia Europe Latin America Middle East Africa's richest man helps fund $660m fuel pipeline between Ethiopia and Djibouti Image source, Bloomberg via Getty Images Image caption, Aliko Dangote made his fortune from cement in Nigeria By Ondiro Oganga Published 25 September 2026 Nigerian billionaire Aliko Dangote has announced that he is helping to fund a new $660m (£500m) fuel pipeline between Ethiopia and Djibouti The project will include a 120km- (75 mile-) pipeline connecting Djibouti's Damerjog port to a distribution facility in Dewele, Ethiopia, as well as storage capacity of about 400 million litres. It is expected to begin operations within 18 months. Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed said the pipeline, which would be a joint venture between Dangote and Ethiopia, is expected to reduce the time needed to transport fuel from Djibouti's port to the Ethiopian capital, Addis Ababa, from five days to one. The first phase will transport key petroleum products, including jet fuel, diesel and petrol. Speaking at the ground-breaking ceremony, Dangote, Africa's richest man, said the project would strengthen Ethiopia's energy security and make its fuel supply chain more resilient. Landlocked Ethiopia relies heavily on Djibouti's port for imports, including petroleum products. The new infrastructure is expected to reduce pressure on existing transport systems supporting industries, including transport, aviation, agriculture and construction. Djibouti is also expected to benefit from increased port activity, job creation and higher government revenues. The project is part of Dangote's wider expansion of infrastructure and manufacturing businesses across Africa. Dangote Cement has production capacity of about 55 million tonnes a year, while his oil refinery in Nigeria currently has capacity to process 700,000 barrels of crude a day and is seeking to double that to 1.4 million barrels a day. The refinery recently listed 4.1 billion ordinary shares on the Nigerian stock exchange, aiming to raise about $1.63bn (£1.2bn). In Kenya, the company is due to break ground next week on a proposed 700,000-barrel-a-day crude oil refinery in Lamu. ethiopia.content: Ethiopia's army says it has repelled TPLF attacks in first comment on fresh Tigray fighting - BBC News BBC Homepage Skip to content Accessibility Help Your account Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds More menu More menu Search BBC Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds Close menu BBC News Menu Home Climate World US & Canada UK Business Tech Science Entertainment & Arts Health More In Pictures BBC Verify Newsbeat World Africa Asia Australia Europe Latin America Middle East Ethiopia's army says it has repelled attacks in first comment on fresh fighting Image source, Reuters Image caption, Tigrayan fighters have been seen on the streets of the region's main city but it is relatively quiet there as clashes flare up elsewhere By Michael Teferi BBC Africa Published 24 September 2026 Ethiopia's army says it has repelled attacks from Tigrayan forces and their allies in parts of the north of the country, in its first statement since fighting broke out on Wednesday. The army said hostilities began in an area of Amhara region close to the border with Tigray, adding that its soldiers had inflicted heavy casualties and seized weapons. The developments come as tensions between the federal government and Tigrayan leaders have sharply escalated over the last few days, raising fears that a devastating civil war could resume. On Wednesday, the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), which dominates the region, seized control of three airports from federal police. The TPLF has not commented on the army's claims and the BBC has not been able to independently verify the army's claims. The BBC is unable to report from Tigray and surrounding areas. There are unconfirmed reports that TPLF forces have launched attacks in the neighbouring regions of Afar and Amhara. A humanitarian source in Afar told AFP news agency on Thursday that Tigrayan forces had launched heavy artillery attacks as they attempted to take control of the town of Yallo, near the border with Tigray. "We are in the situation of full-blown war now," TPLF vice-president Amanuel Assefa is quoted by the news agency as saying. The latest escalation follows months of rising tensions between Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's government and Tigray authorities, who fought a devastating war from 2020 to 2022. That ended in an African Union-brokered peace deal but over recent months both sides have been accusing each other of violating the agreement. It was one of the most deadly conflicts this century - the AU's mediator estimated some 600,000 people died as the fighting drove the region to the precipice of famine. On Sunday, the TPLF announced an alliance with six other armed groups to oust the government. Following the seizure of the airports, Ethiopian Airlines has cancelled all flights to Tigray. Residents of Tigray's main city of Mekelle told the BBC that local forces had taken over control of the city's airport from the national police early on Wednesday. This followed reports of drone strikes in Tigray in recent days. A Mekelle resident told the BBC's Newsday programme on Thursday there had been no clashes in the city, unlike in the previous war, with most fighting happening elsewhere. Figure caption, Tigray capital 'out of cash' as fighting escalates "Mekelle is calm, except the stress from the people," said the resident, only identified as Fitsum for his safety. He added that the biggest problem was economic, with people not having enough cash. "People are in a mood where they are distressed because it's been so difficult, so tough. The last seven or eight months the government has been denying budgets to the civil servants and all the banks were running out of cash." Fitsum said people had been relying on mobile banking but with the risk of communications being cut off, "people are going to be in grave danger because there is almost no cash". With the outbreak of war, people were limiting their movements and the city was all quiet - "it's like a curfew has been placed," he told the BBC. ethiopia.content: Ethiopia and Tigray accuse each other of launching offensives, fuelling fears of new war - BBC News BBC Homepage Skip to content Accessibility Help Your account Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds More menu More menu Search BBC Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds Close menu BBC News Menu Home Climate World US & Canada UK Business Tech Science Entertainment & Arts Health More In Pictures BBC Verify Newsbeat World Africa Asia Australia Europe Latin America Middle East Ethiopia and Tigray accuse each other of launching offensives, fuelling fears of new war Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, TPLF fighters were patrolling the streets of Mekelle on Wednesday By Teklemariam Bekit BBC Tigrinya Published 23 September 2026 Updated 24 September 2026 Ethiopia's government and the party in control of the northern region of Tigray have accused each other of launching offensives, escalating fears of a return to full-scale conflict. Getachew Reda, a cabinet minister and adviser to Ethiopia's prime minister, said Tigrayan fighters had taken control of federally administered airports in Tigray and launched offensives in neighbouring Afar and Amhara regions. Earlier, the Tigrayan authorities said their forces had been forced to enter a "defensive war". The statement followed reports of drone strikes in Tigray. The two-year war in Tigray ended in 2022 - but over recent months both sides have been accusing each other of violating a peace deal. It was one of the most deadly conflicts this century - the African Union's mediator estimated some 600,000 people died as the fighting drove the region to the precipice of famine. Speaking at the UN General Assembly, Ethiopian President Taye Astike Selassie said his country had shown "immense restraint" in its actions despite "interference in our internal affairs by adversarial elements", without specifying who those elements were. He added: "Our message to forces of destruction and mayhem is loud and clear. We urge them to respect the sacred right of the people of the Horn of Africa to live in peace and prosperity." On Sunday, the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), the party that runs Tigray, announced an alliance with six other armed groups in Ethiopia to remove the government in Addis Ababa. Seven Ethiopian rebel groups form new alliance Published 21 September Getachew said in a statement shared on social media: "It is rather heartbreaking to learn that, despite efforts by many, including the international community, to avoid yet another round of war in Tigray, the TPLF leadership early this morning launched an all-out offensive against government positions in Afar and Amhara." The adviser to Prime Minster Abiy Ahmed previously led Tigray's interim administration, but he fell out with the TPLF in 2025 and joined the federal government. Following the seizure of the airports, Ethiopian Airlines has cancelled all flights to Tigray. Residents of Tigray's main city of Mekelle told the BBC that local forces had taken over control of the city's airport from the national police early on Wednesday. This followed reports of drone strikes in Tigray in recent days. A resident of Mekelle told the BBC's Newsday programme there had been no clashes in the city, unlike in the previous war, with most fighting happening elsewhere. "Mekelle is calm, except the stress from the people," said the resident, only identified as Fitsum for his safety. He added that the biggest problem was economic, with people not having enough cash. "People are in a mood where they are distressed because it's been so difficult, so tough. The last seven or eight months the government has been denying budgets to the civil servants and all the banks were running out of cash." Fitsum said people had been relying on mobile banking but with the risk of communications being cut off, "people are going to be in grave danger because there is almost no cash". With the outbreak of war, people were limiting their movements and the city was all quiet - "it's like a curfew has been placed," he told the BBC. The chairperson of the Africa Union Commission, Mahmoud Ali Youssouf, has called for an "immediate de-escalation" and for both sides to resume talks. The US ambassador to Ethiopia condemned the TPLF for making "the poor decision to launch a large-scale offensive", describing it as an "unwinnable fight". On Tuesday, a strike in the southern town of Alamata killed at least 14 people and injured 22 others, according to the Tigrayan authorities. The town's mayor, Mogos Shiferaw, told the BBC that more than five drones and one fighter jet had carried out more than 21 strikes starting at around 03:30. "This caused a lot of psychological trauma in our city and our people were in a state of panic," he said. Mogos said all those killed and injured were civilians, accusing federal forces of targeting two secondary schools. He believed they were struck on suspicion that they were being used by Tigrayan forces. But the mayor said the schools, which had served as federal military bases during the civil war, were unoccupied as the academic year had not yet begun. The BBC has not independently verified the allegations and the government has not commented on the alleged strikes. On Wednesday, the Tigray authorities accused Addis Ababa of launching an "open invasion" of the region, urging people to support the regional forces and maintain unity. It further accused the government of violating international humanitarian and human rights laws, saying public services and critical infrastructure had been disrupted. Meanwhile, the US State Department's Bureau of African Affairs has condemned a separate drone strike that it said took place on Monday, targeting a convoy of Catholic vehicles carrying food aid. It called for an investigation and urged all parties to resolve their differences through dialogue and take steps to prevent similar incidents. Both Addis Ababa and TPLF leaders have faced criticism over delays in implementing key provisions of the Pretoria Agreement, the AU-brokered deal that formally ended the conflict in November 2022. In July, Prime Minister Abiy accused the TPLF of preparing for renewed conflict during an address to parliament. Just before the general election in May, which was not held in Tigray because of the security situation, the TPLF restored its pre-war administration, disbanding an interim one appointed by Abiy. There have also been reports that the TPLF has been forcibly recruiting young men to join its forces. ethiopia.content: Ethiopia conflict: Seven armed groups form alliance against Abiy Ahmed - BBC News BBC Homepage Skip to content Accessibility Help Your account Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds More menu More menu Search BBC Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds Close menu BBC News Menu Home Climate World US & Canada UK Business Tech Science Entertainment & Arts Health More In Pictures BBC Verify Newsbeat World Africa Asia Australia Europe Latin America Middle East Seven Ethiopian rebel groups form new alliance Image source, Reuters Image caption, There have been renewed tensions in the northern Tigray region By Michael Teferi and Basillioh Rukanga Published 21 September 2026 Several of the rebel groups which have been fighting the Ethiopian authorities in different parts of the country have announced they have formed an alliance to remove the government in Addis Ababa. The alliance brings together the Fano militia in Amhara, the Oromo Liberation Army (OLA), Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) and four other smaller groupings in a coalition named Alliance for Survival. The seven groups accuse Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's government of presiding over "war, genocide, mass destruction and utter poverty", claiming Ethiopia is at risk of disintegration. Abiy's spokesperson Billene Seyoum said the groups had already been collaborating for some time, Reuters reports. The BBC has asked the government for comment. Ethiopia has faced years of armed conflict in Oromia and Amhara, the most populous states in the country. There have also been renewed tensions in the northern Tigray region, where a two-year civil war left hundreds of thousands dead and displaced millions. An African-Union peace deal ended that war in 2022, but there have been fears of a return to a full-scale conflict, with both sides accusing each other of violating that agreement. Besides Oromia, Amhara and Tigray, the new alliance also includes groups based in three other regions - Somali, Afar and Benishangul-Gumuz – making up a half of Ethiopia's 12 regional states. The states are structured largely based on their dominant ethnic groups – a system of ethnic federalism that gives some autonomy to the states, but which can present social and political challenges for the country which has more than 80 ethnic groups. Some of the rebel groups in the new alliance have previously fought against each other but they say they will now work together against their common enemy. However, analyst Edward Bach from advisory firm Verisk Maplecroft told the AFP news agency that the groups were "unlikely to share weapons... as your ally today can be your enemy tomorrow". Amhara's Fano group fought alongside federal forces against the TPLF during the Tigray war. It however turned against the federal government in an armed insurgency less than a year after the war ended, after refusing government orders to disarm. Abdikadir Addaani Hirmooge, the spokesman for the Ogaden National Liberation Front (ONLF), which is part of the alliance, told the BBC that the groups in the new coalition were working to bring together communities that have been divided against one another. "Our objective is for the communities to have democracy and to exercise their right to self-determination, to genuinely govern themselves," he said. He said that the government had not respected a peace deal signed in 2018 to end the conflict in the Somali region. "Ethnic conflict, insecurity, and mutual oppression and pushing each other aside have not been eradicated, resulting in a need that has affected every ethnic group," he said. The government has been fighting the OLA since 2018. The announcement of the Alliance for Survival coalition comes months after reports of an alleged alliance between TPLF and neighbouring Eritrea. Abiy responded by saying he had faith in Ethiopia's "defensive capabilities". "Even if others were added, we do not have an iota of fear regarding Ethiopia's sovereignty," he told lawmakers in July. The country held a general election in June, with Abiy's Prosperity Party retaining its overwhelming parliamentary majority, despite the poll being overshadowed by conflict, accusations of repression and little participation by opposition parties. The Fano and OLA rebel groups rejected the election and its results. The Tigray region and its six million inhabitants were completely excluded from the poll. ethiopia.content: Afcon 2028: Ethiopia submits official bid to host tournament in East Africa - BBC Sport BBC Homepage Skip to content Accessibility Help Your account Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds More menu More menu Search BBC Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds Close menu BBC Sport Menu Home Football Cricket Formula 1 Rugby U Tennis Golf Cycling Athletics More A-Z Sports American Football Athletics Basketball Boxing Cricket Cycling Darts Disability Sport Football Formula 1 Gaelic Games Golf Gymnastics Horse Racing Mixed Martial Arts Motorsport Netball Rugby League Rugby Union Snooker Swimming Tennis Full Sports A-Z More from Sport England Scotland Wales Northern Ireland Quizzes News Feeds Help & FAQs Sport Africa Ethiopia submits official bid to host Afcon 2028 Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Ethiopia, ranked 143rd in the world and 43rd in Africa, have qualified for Afcon only three times since they last hosted in 1976, most recently playing at the delayed 2021 edition Published 25 August 2026 Ethiopia has submitted an official bid to host the 2028 Africa Cup of Nations (Afcon). The country's football federation (EFF) says its government-backed proposal affirms "the nation's full readiness to host Africa's biggest footballing event". Ethiopia has staged Afcon three times, in 1962, 1968 and 1976, but its footballing infrastructure lags well behind others on the continent. The nation had just one stadium approved for use by the Confederation of African Football (Caf) last season but is in the process of inaugurating a new international stadium and sports complex in Addis Ababa. That venue in the capital could provide one location for the tournament, but whether Ethiopia has enough compliant venues to host a 24-team Afcon across multiple locations remains a major question. A number of existing regional facilities are understood not to meet Fifa or Caf standards in terms of infrastructure, facilities and overall match-day requirements. Ethiopia played its home qualifiers for the 2026 Fifa World Cup at neutral venues in Morocco and Rwanda but did host matches in Dire Dawa earlier this year. Last month, Caf president Patrice Motsepe said his organisation had received "exciting bids" for the 2028, 2032 and 2036 Afcons - with the tournament set to move to a four-year cycle after 2028 . Botswana, Namibia, South Africa and Zimbabwe announced a joint Southern African bid for the 2028 finals earlier this year. Despite reports that Morocco - hosts of the 2025 edition - could stage the tournament again in two years' time, BBC Sport Africa understands the kingdom is not in the running and instead is focusing on preparations to co-host the 2030 Fifa World Cup. Meanwhile, Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger - three countries led by military governments - have expressed interest in co-hosting in 2032. The 2027 Afcon is scheduled to take place in Kenya, Tanzania and Uganda from 19 June to 17 July next year, with the competition returning to East Africa for the first time since it was held in Ethiopia in 1976. Ethiopia won the Afcon title on home soil in 1962 but the Walia Ibex, ranked 143rd in the world and 43rd in Africa, have only qualified for the tournament three times since they last hosted. Their most recent appearance came at the 2021 edition, when they finished bottom without a win in a group containing Cameroon, Burkina Faso and Cape Verde. Ethiopia beat Sao Tome and Principe in the preliminary round of qualifiers for next year's Afcon and have been drawn alongside Senegal, Mozambique and Sudan in Group J. Is holding Afcon every four years 'totally wrong' or 'good call'? Published 22 January Infrastructure and security concerns Analysis by Kaleb Moges, BBC Africa The EFF's announcement that it wants to host Afcon has generated mixed reactions, with critics questioning whether the country is truly prepared to host a tournament of this scale. Ethiopia was one of just three nations to play at the first Afcon in 1957, but the 52,000-seat Bahir Dar Stadium in the north of the country is currently the only facility it posseses which is approved by Caf. Meanwhile, the 62,000-capacity Adey Abeba International Stadium in Addis Ababa is expected to be completed next year. Three other proposed stadiums are at much earlier stages of development and would need significant work to meet Caf's requirements in time for 2028. However, hosting Afcon would require more than upgrading or constructing stadiums. The country would also need adequate training facilities, gyms, accommodation and entertainment venues, as well as reliable urban transport and security infrastructure. Security is a major concern for Ethiopia's bid. Although the capital city is comparatively safe, several parts of the country continue to experience armed conflict, political unrest and other security challenges. Addressing these concerns, alongside the infrastructure requirements, would be critical if Ethiopia is to successfully host Afcon 2028. # وهذا على، ما اعتقد، يعتبر قصورا اداريا واضحا، لا علاقة له بدور الجهاز الفني، او العناصر التي شملها الاختيار من اللاعبين بالقائمة.. وعلينا هنا الاتفاق اولا على هذه الجزئية، قبل مواصلة تناول تفاصيل السقوط الذي كشف واثبت الفشل.. # يعلم الجميع، ومنذ سنوات، ان مباريات التصفيات – سواء المؤهلة لامم افريقيا، او المونديال – تقام معظم مبارياتها خلال ايام معدودة.. حيث لعبت كل المنتخبات مباراتين خلال أسبوع واحد بالتصفيات الحالية.. # برنامج هذه التصفيات، صدر من جانب الكاف قبل شهور من الان (مايو الماضي).. واعتقد ان تلك المدة او الفترة الزمنية كانت كافية لقادة جميع الإتحادات، للترتيب بالصورة المناسبة لمباريات منتخباتها، ولو بالقدر الذي يجنب لاعبيهم الإرهاق، ويؤمن لهم اداء الجولات بالصورة المطلوبة بصرف النظر عن الفوز والخسارة.. # لكن للأسف، وعلى الرغم من إننا تابعنا الإهتمام والتنسيق وهو يحدث من جانب كل اتحادات القارة السمراء.. الا ان اتحادنا الهمام، فشل في القيام بالمهمة الأساسية التي بموجبها وصل قادته وجلسوا على كراسي حكم وادارة الكرة السودانية.. # نعود إلى الخسارة، التي عصفت بمنتخبنا من صدارة المجموعة التاسعة، الي المركز الثالث (قبل الأخير) بالمجموعة. حيث انفردت موزمبيق بالمركز الأول، يليه السنغال ولكل اربع نقاط، مع أفضلية لموزمبيق بالأهداف.. ثم السودان بثلاث نقاط.. واخيرا إثيوبيا يلا رصيد.. # الحقيقة، ان الهزيمة خلطت حسابات منتخبنا، وصعبت مهمته في التأهل للنهائيات المقبلة، المقررة العام القادم بكل من تنزانيا وكينيا ويوغندا.. وصار لزاما علينا الفوز على الاقل في لقاء واحد بالجولتين القادمتين امام السنغال..!! # والسعي، بعدها لعبور إثيوبيا في الجولة الخامسة، ثم حسم الثلاث نقاط امام موزمبيق بالجولة السادسة والاخيرة..بجانب انتظار تعثر موزمبيق واثيوبيا.. ويا لها من مهمة صعبة وَمعقدة، ربما تمهد لفشلنا، وتقطع علينا طريق النهائيات، وبالتالي نعود للتقوقع مرة أخرى..!! # والتقوقع الذي أعنيه هنا علاقته مباشرة بالغياب عن مسرح نهائيات الأمم الأفريقية، التي اعتدنا على الظهور فيها خلال السنوات الأخيرة.. وعلى الرغم من إننا نفشل في تحقيق النتائج المرجوة، الا ان توجدنا كان يضعنا دوما داخل إطار الصورة التنافسية.. # انها واحدة من (الهفوات القاتلة) التي ظلت الجماعة الحالية تدمن الوقوع فيها.. وللأسف يبقى السودان ومنتخباته هي الجهة الوحيدة التي تدفع الثمن غاليا، حيث تخصم الهزائم من اسم بلادنا وسمعتها ومكانتها، التي اهتزت كثيرا خلال السنوات الأخيرة، في ظل تخبطات هذه المجموعة الفاشلة.. # *تخريمة اولى:* سالني احد الأصدقاء من شمال، شاهد مباراة مصر الثلاثاء امام جنوب السودان بجوبا وقال لي: (هو جنوب السودان عندهم ملعب.. وانتو في الشمال ما عندكمش ملعب)..؟!! # *تخريمة ثانية:* الجمني ذلك السؤال، وَتحججت له بالحرب اللعينة التي قاربت إكمال أربع سنوات.. قلت ذلك وانا أعلم أن الحرب بريئة من ذلك، ولاعلاقة لها البتة بقصة غياب ملعب قانوني في سودان عطا المنان..!! # *تخريمة ثالثة:* تقدمت جماعة التدمير بشكوى، طاعنة في قانونية مشاركة احد لاعبي موزمبيق.. وبناء على ذلك طالبوا بالنقاط.. (لقد نقلوا الشكاوى المحلية والبسوها ثوب الدولية).. حكمتك يا رب..!! # *حاجة اخيرة:* ما فعلته جماعة عطا المنان في صقور الجديان كووووم.. والصدامات التي حدث عقب الهزيمة المرة بين الجماهير.. كووووم تااااني خالص.. (انه التعصب الذي اعمى القلوب والابصار).. لك الله يا وطني..!! # *همسة:* عشرات الأجانب في المريخ والهلال.. وبعد ده كلو يجيك واحد يقول ليك: (المنتخب هلالي.. وشعاره مريخي).. حليلك يا بروف شداد.. والتحية ليك من على البعد..!! # *همسة خاصة:* سالناك يا اسامة قبل أيام.. وها نحن نعيد وتكرر سؤالنا: (اها.. كيف “العمل”)..؟؟!! # *همسة خاصة جدا:* اوعى تقول لي ح تستقيلووا.. والله ما بصدقكم نهائي. لان جلدكم بقي تخيين.. ووشكم مكشوف ومجلد..!! # *همسة خاصة جدا جدا:* للأسف فإن (مرارات بعض أفراد القطيع) هي التي تجعل أصواتهم عالية.. مثلها ممثل (البراميل الفارغة)..!! (الجنوب عندهم ملعب.. وانتو لا)..؟!! 215 مشاركة المقال قد يعجبك أيضا مقالات كورة ((لم يعد السكوت ممكنا فقد بلغ السيل الذبى؟؟)) مقالات كورة اتحاد 4G مقالات كورة هزيمة مُذلّة.. يتحمل مسؤوليتها اتحاد الكرة والإطار الفني مقالات كورة ((ليس موزمبيق بل أسامه وجعفر؟؟)) السابق التالي اترك رد إلغاء الرد لن يتم نشر عنوان بريدك الإلكتروني. احفظ اسمي والبريد الإلكتروني وموقع الويب في هذا المتصفح للمرة الأولى التي أعلق فيها. أخبار الحوادث فزع يستعيد مركبة منهوبة بعد ساعات من نهبها… الدلنج تشهد تطورات خطيرة:الحلو يعرض حياة أكثر… هل وطئت أقدام الجنجويد أرضاً عمروها؟ حادث مروري بطريق المرور السريع كسلا يؤدي الي… مكافحة المخدرات تلقي القبض على أخطر تاجر… ضبط اكثر من 2000 قندول بنقو بالفولة السابق التالي 1 من 376 منوعات كورة تهنئة للطالب أحمد عمر بشاشة بمناسبة نجاحه في… ((الأعلامية محاسن تستدرج الفنان القلع)) بمناسبة مرور عام على تحرير أبوعشر (٨) بمناسبة مرور عام على تحرير أبوعشر (٧) بمناسبة مرور عام على تحرير أبوعشر (٦) بمناسبة مرور عام على تحرير أبوعشر (٥) السابق التالي 1 من 271 المزيد من المقالات ((لم يعد السكوت ممكنا فقد بلغ السيل الذبى؟؟)) اتحاد 4G هزيمة مُذلّة.. يتحمل مسؤوليتها اتحاد الكرة والإطار الفني السابق التالي 1 من 5٬988 عن الموقع للإعلان معنا الاتصال بنا خريطة الموقع سياسة الخصوصية © 2026 - صحيفة كورة سودانية الإلكترونية. التركيب والاستضافة من كريستا هوست يستخدم هذا الموقع ملفات تعريف الارتباط لتحسين تجربتك. سنفترض أنك موافق على ذلك ، ولكن يمكنك إلغاء الاشتراك إذا كنت ترغب في ذلك. قبول قراءة المزيد
